revisions.body: Critias’s distinction is sharper than the claim that only noble and beneficial acts count as “work.” He says that work is never a reproach; rather, noble and beneficial works are the ones he classifies as one’s own, while harmful works are alien. That move turns “doing one’s own” into doing good things. Socrates does not resolve the terminology. He grants Critias freedom to choose his names, then asks him to state the resulting definition plainly: temperance is the doing or making of good things. One way to read the passage is as a shift from ownership to evaluation.

Socrates has required a science to have something distinct as its subject. Critias now makes temperance the exception: it is a science of the other sciences and of itself, and Socrates extends that answer to include non-knowledge. Does this identify a subject matter, or only rename self-reference as knowledge?

The thought experiment separates the crafts themselves from the knowledge that makes their results beneficial. Critias’s answer is not that knowledge of good and bad performs every technical task; it is that doing well and being happy require this one knowledge rather than knowledgeable living in general or the sum of the other crafts. That distinction is the hinge: technical expertise can remain intact while the question of its good use comes into view.

The Republic offers a useful contrast, not a final verdict on this passage. At 442d, sōphrosynē is described as agreement that the rational part rules, a condition of inner order rather than knowledge of knowledge. Since this account uses different premises, the Charmides refutation does not directly address it. The comparison broadens the question without closing the aporia.

body: "Cornered, Critias escapes by changing what the words mean. Leaning on a line of Hesiod, he splits making from doing and working, so that only things done nobly and beneficially count as real work — and only those count as one's own. Ownership quietly becomes goodness: doing your own business now means doing good things. Socrates lets the wordplay pass, comparing it to Prodicus's endless distinctions between names, and asks only that Critias say plainly what he means. The result is a genuinely new definition: temperance is the doing of good things."

body: "Critias’s answer makes knowledge of good and bad the single knowledge connected with doing well and being happy, rather than merely the sum of all technical know-how. Socrates marks this shift with a personal accusation: he says Critias has been leading him in circles and concealing the answer. That is Socrates’ charge, not proof of Critias’ intention. He then tests the distinction by asking whether the other crafts would lose their own work if this knowledge were removed. They would not. The pressure point is therefore not whether each craft can perform its task, but what makes its result beneficial."
